claims.text: Resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in HEA multilayer coatings arises from a synergistic effect of compositional disorder and engineered multilayer interfaces.
The coating consists of nanoscale alternating HEA layers.
The as-deposited multilayer coating is initially in a low-defect state.
Engineered interfaces and compositional complexity promote the formation of misfit dislocation networks.
Misfit dislocation networks pin mobile dislocations.
Differences in lattice parameters across multilayer interfaces produce misfit strain.
Differences in elastic moduli across multilayer interfaces contribute to localized stress fields.
Localized interfacial stress fields lock or impede dislocations.
Multilayer interfaces impede both dislocation glide and dislocation climb.
Impeded dislocation glide and climb slow or prevent creep deformation.
Under identical creep conditions, a multilayer HEA coating will exhibit lower creep strain than a homogeneous HEA coating of the same overall composition.
Under identical creep conditions, dislocation mobility will be lower in the multilayer HEA coating than in the homogeneous coating.
The proposed mechanism applies below temperatures and stresses that induce microstructural transformations such as recrystallization.
The proposed mechanism applies when individual layers remain nanoscale and interface effects dominate.
Direct microstructural evidence linking specific dislocation-interface interactions to creep resistance is currently lacking.
